title: October 2026 CPI Has No 12-Month Rate: Test Every CPI Escalation Clause in Your Leases, Vendor Contracts, and COLAs From the Books Before the First Invoice Reprices
excerpt: BLS releases the October 2026 CPI today without a 12-month change for all items or core, because October 2025 prices were never collected. Here is how a finance team inventories every CPI escalation clause across leases, vendor and customer contracts, and wage COLAs, sorts the ones that break from the ones that don't, prices the fallback values, books the uplift under ASC 842, and resets the 2027 budget assumption.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: Finance team mapping every CPI escalation clause in a lease and contract register against the BLS CPI table with a dash in the October 2025 column
content:
The October 2026 CPI report lands today with no 12-month inflation rate for all items or core, because BLS never collected October 2025 prices. Every CPI escalation clause that measures October to October points at a missing number. Finance teams need to find each one in leases, vendor contracts, and COLAs and pick a value before invoices reprice.

Why this matters now

The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October 2026 Consumer Price Index at 8:30 a.m. Eastern today, November 10, according to its release schedule. Its shutdown impact FAQ, updated 2026-09-16, states the problem in one sentence: 'BLS will not publish 12-month percent changes for October 2026 for indexes where October 2025 data are not available.' The reason is a year old. During the lapse in appropriations that ran from October 1 to November 12, 2025, the agency 'could not collect October 2025 reference period survey data.' It carried September 2025 survey prices forward to October, carried April 2025 rents forward so the rent and owners' equivalent rent indexes were unchanged for October, and never issued an October 2025 CPI release. In the published tables, October 2025 is a dash.

The November 2025 CPI release of 2025-12-18 shows what that looks like in practice. It reported a 0.2 percent seasonally adjusted change over the two months from September to November 2025, a 12-month all-items increase of 2.7 percent, and a core increase of 2.6 percent, with the October column marked unavailable. A BLS Monthly Labor Review article of 2026-05-12 later estimated that the carried-forward rents understated the published 12-month rent change, 3.02 percent against 3.27 to 3.56 percent under alternative methods, with the gap closing by April 2026. So the November 2025 figures exist, but they carry a known bias that matters if you plan to use them as a substitute base.

Today's report will still contain the monthly changes. The StockTitan preview of 2026-11-06 puts consensus at 0.3 percent for headline and core on an unadjusted basis, with the Cleveland Fed nowcast at 0.24 and 0.21 percent, and notes that gasoline, new vehicles, and used cars keep their 12-month comparisons because BLS obtained that October 2025 data from non-survey sources. The last official 12-month all-items figure is September's 3.7 percent. Investing.com reported on 2026-09-11, citing BLS spokesperson Cody Parkinson, that year-over-year real earnings will be missing for the same reason.

The market coverage stops there. One contract-intelligence vendor, Acrebase, published a September 25, 2026 note on leases whose reference month is October, showing three candidate values for the missing index and a spread of roughly half a percentage point of rent between them. That is useful, and it is also only one contract type. What a finance team needs is a way to run every CPI-linked clause it holds, as tenant, landlord, buyer, seller, and employer, through the same test, pick a value for each, book it, and reset the 2027 budget assumption. That is this article.

Which CPI escalation clauses break today, and which don't

Contracts don't use the seasonally adjusted monthly change the headlines quote. They use not seasonally adjusted index levels, or a published 12-month percent change, for a named index and a named month. Three questions sort every clause: which index (CPI-U, CPI-W, or a regional series), which measurement (an index ratio, a published percent change, or an annual average), and which reference month. Only clauses that need an October 2025 value, or the October 2026 12-month change, are affected. The rest work exactly as they did last year.

Clause wordingWhat it needsStatus todayWhat to do
The percentage change in CPI-U for the twelve months ending OctoberA published 12-month figureBroken: BLS will not publish itNegotiate a substitute: September's 3.7 percent, a 13-month change scaled to twelve months, or wait for November to November on December 10
CPI-U for October 2026 divided by CPI-U for October 2025Two index levelsBroken: October 2025 is a dashSubstitute the base: November 2025 (324.122), the September and November average (324.461), or the Treasury formula value (325.604)
The most recent 12-month change published as of the adjustment dateWhatever is currentWorks, but ambiguousFor a November or December adjustment it resolves to September's figure; write a file note saying so
September to September, or November to NovemberTwo published index levelsWorksSeptember was published in October 2026; November publishes December 10, 2026
The lesser of the CPI change or a cap, such as 3 percentEither of the aboveDepends on the capCompute every candidate; if all exceed the cap, the cap binds and the choice is moot
A sublease or customer contract that mirrors a head lease on OctoberThe same missing base, on both sidesBroken twiceUse the same substitute on both sides so the margin is preserved

Two features of the table deserve a second look. First, a floating clause that says the most recent 12-month change published as of the adjustment date is not broken, but it is ambiguous: for a December 1 adjustment the most recent published 12-month change is September's, and the file should say so. Second, a cap changes the question. If a lease says the lesser of the CPI change or 3 percent, and every candidate value produces more than 3 percent, the cap binds and the choice of substitute is moot. Compute all the candidates before opening a negotiation you may not need.

One company, fourteen clauses: the walk-through

Call it Ridgeline Components: three operating entities, about $48 million of revenue, a lease register built for ASC 842, and a controller who read the BLS FAQ in September and did nothing, because October felt far away. The figures are illustrative. The sequence is not.

Step one: inventory every CPI-linked clause

The lease register lists the leases but not which ones carry index escalators, so the controller pulls every lease abstract, every supplier agreement with a pricing schedule, every customer master services agreement, and the collective bargaining agreement at the plant. Fourteen clauses reference a consumer price index: six leases where Ridgeline is the tenant, two subleases where it is the landlord, three supplier agreements, two customer agreements, and one wage COLA. A company that keeps its lease schedule and ASC 842 entries in one place finds the six leases in minutes. The other eight live in a contracts folder nobody reports from.

Step two: classify by index, measurement, and month

Nine of the fourteen are fine. Four leases adjust on their January, March, and June anniversaries using those months' indexes. Two supplier agreements use September to September, and September's index was published in October 2026. The COLA uses the CPI-W 12-month change for September, which BLS published. Two clauses float to the most recent published 12-month figure as of a December 1 adjustment, which resolves to September's 3.7 percent and needs a file note rather than a negotiation.

Five are broken. Two leases, one supplier agreement, and one customer agreement divide the October 2026 CPI-U by the October 2025 CPI-U. One sublease mirrors its head lease, so it is broken on both sides at once. The controller writes down the exact wording of each substitution clause. All five say the parties will substitute a comparable index if the CPI is discontinued or revised. None says what happens when the index exists and a single month in it does not, which is the gap the Acrebase note identified for leases.

Step three: price every candidate value

For the index-ratio clauses the missing input is the October 2025 CPI-U. The series around the gap, as the Acrebase note lays it out, reads 324.800 for September 2025, a dash for October, and 324.122 for November. Three substitutes are on the table. Use November's 324.122, the first published value after the gap. Use the average of September and November, 324.461. Or use the method the Treasury applies to inflation-protected securities when a CPI month is not reported, set out in 31 CFR Part 356, Appendix B: grow the prior month's index at the monthly rate implied by the last available 12-month change, which gives 325.604. The gap between the lowest and highest base is about 0.46 percent of the escalation ratio, so on the $900,000 lease it is about $4,100 of annual rent, and on the $1.4 million lease about $6,400. Each side of the negotiation will prefer a different base, and the controller records all three before the call.

The two broken leases both carry a 3 percent cap. If October 2026 comes in anywhere near September's 3.7 percent annual pace, every one of the three bases produces more than 3 percent, the cap binds, and the base question answers itself. That leaves the supplier agreement, the customer agreement, and the sublease, where the money is real and the sides are reversed. On the supplier agreement Ridgeline prefers the highest base, because a higher October 2025 denominator means a smaller increase. On the customer agreement and the sublease it prefers the lowest. Picking one method and applying it consistently across all five is the defensible position, and it is also the one a reviewer can test.

Step four: book what you know before the invoices agree

The accounting does not wait for the counterparty. For the leases where Ridgeline is tenant, the rent increase from a change in CPI is a variable lease payment. Under ASC 842, as PwC's Viewpoint guide updated 2026-07-23 explains, a change in a reference index does not resolve a contingency and does not trigger remeasurement of the lease liability, so the increase is recognized as variable lease cost in the period it is incurred. If the landlord has not invoiced because the base is in dispute, Ridgeline accrues its best estimate anyway: debit variable lease cost, credit accrued rent payable, and true up when the number is agreed. For the sublease it records the mirror image when the amount is determinable. For the customer agreement the uplift is variable consideration under ASC 606 and is estimated and constrained. For the supplier agreement the controller accrues the expected uplift on receipts after the adjustment date. For the COLA, payroll gets the September CPI-W figure, which exists, on the contract's effective date.

Step five: fix the 2027 budget assumption

Ridgeline's budget model indexed next year's occupancy and material costs to the October 12-month CPI. That cell is now empty. The controller replaces it with a documented choice: September's 3.7 percent as the last official annual rate, or, once today's index level is published, the 13-month change from September 2025 to October 2026 scaled to twelve months, labeled as a derived figure and not a BLS statistic. The November report on December 10 will restore a clean 12-month comparison, and the model should be built to swap it in, the same way a cash forecast rebuilt after a rate change carries the reset date in the file. A budget versus actual variance explained by a changed inflation input is a different conversation from one explained by a bad estimate, and the file should make the difference visible.

Step six: the one-page memo per clause

Each of the fourteen clauses gets one page: the contract, the index, the measurement, the reference month, whether it is affected, the three candidate values where it is, the value chosen and why, the cap if any, the counterparty's position, the entry booked, and the owner. Nine of the pages are two lines long. Five are the reason the memo exists.

Accounting controls for CPI escalation clauses with a missing index

Source data: the lease register and each lease abstract with the escalation and substitution wording; supplier and customer contracts with pricing schedules; the collective bargaining agreement; the BLS CPI tables for the named index, not seasonally adjusted, with the published values for September 2025, November 2025, and October 2026 once released, and the dash for October 2025 recorded as a fact; the September 2026 12-month change for CPI-U and CPI-W; the BLS FAQ and the November 2025 release as the authority for why the month is missing; and the 2027 budget model's inflation input cells.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Classify each clause by index, measurement, and reference month. Flag only the clauses that need an October 2025 value or the October 2026 12-month change. For each flagged clause compute the escalation under all three candidate bases and under the cap. Apply one method consistently. The rent uplift is a flow item: variable lease cost in the income statement for the periods after the adjustment date, debit expense and credit cash or accrued liabilities. The accrued liability is a point-in-time balance that must agree to the sum of uplifts incurred and not yet paid. The lease liability and right-of-use asset are not remeasured for an index change alone. On the revenue side the uplift is variable consideration, estimated and constrained, debit receivable or contract asset and credit revenue. Never net the tenant and landlord sides of a mirrored sublease; book each gross so the margin is visible.

Review: a second person confirms each clause's classification against the contract wording, not the abstract; confirms that the index values used are the not seasonally adjusted series the contract names; recomputes the three candidate values and the cap test; confirms the same method was applied to every flagged clause whether it helps or hurts; ties the accrued rent payable and the receivable to the memo; and confirms the budget model's inflation input is labeled with its source and will be replaced when the November report publishes a 12-month figure.

Decision: the controller owns the classification and the entries. The CFO owns the choice of substitute method and the decision to apply it consistently, because that choice moves cash in both directions. Legal owns the reading of the substitution clause and any amendment. The counterparty owns its agreement, and until it is given the entry stands at Ridgeline's best estimate with the memo attached.

Limits and common mistakes

Do not wait for an October 2025 value to appear. The November 2025 release said BLS was unable to retroactively collect the data, and the FAQ shows the month as a dash. A clause that points at it needs a substitute, not patience.

Do not use the seasonally adjusted monthly changes from the news release to settle a contract. Escalators run on not seasonally adjusted index levels, and the two series move differently in October.

The November 2025 values carry a known bias. BLS's own May 2026 analysis estimated that carried-forward rents understated the published rent change by a quarter to half a point. A November base is a legitimate choice, but it is not a neutral one.

The Treasury formula is a rule for inflation-protected securities, not for private contracts. It is a reference point both sides can verify, and nothing more, unless the contract adopts it.

Clauses that are fine on paper still need a file note. A floating most-recent-published clause resolves differently depending on the adjustment date, and a reviewer six months from now needs to see which report was current.

Ridgeline is illustrative. The index values, dates, and BLS methodology come from the BLS FAQ, the November 2025 release, the Monthly Labor Review article, and the Acrebase and PwC sources cited above. Whether a substitution clause reaches a missing month is a legal question for the contract and the jurisdiction.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the October 2026 CPI report have no 12-month inflation rate?

BLS could not collect October 2025 prices during the lapse in appropriations that ran from October 1 to November 12, 2025, carried September prices forward to compute November, and never published October 2025 index values. Without an October 2025 base there is no 12-month comparison for October 2026, so BLS will publish only the monthly changes for all items and core, plus 12-month changes for the few components, such as gasoline and vehicles, where it obtained October 2025 data from non-survey sources.

Does a CPI escalation clause that references October still work?

Only if it does not need an October 2025 value or the October 2026 12-month change. A clause that divides the October 2026 index by the October 2025 index, or that applies the published 12-month change for October, has no input to use. A clause that uses September, November, or another month, or that floats to the most recent published figure, works as before. Check the exact wording, because most substitution language covers a discontinued or revised index and not a single missing month.

What value can replace the missing October 2025 index in a lease or contract?

Three candidates are commonly discussed: the November 2025 index of 324.122, the first published value after the gap; the average of the September and November 2025 values, 324.461; and the Treasury method for inflation-protected securities, which grows the September index at the monthly rate implied by the last available 12-month change and gives 325.604. The spread is about 0.46 percent of the escalation ratio. Compute all three, test them against any cap, apply one method consistently, and document the counterparty's agreement.

How does a tenant account for a CPI rent increase under ASC 842?

As variable lease cost in the period the increase is incurred. Under ASC 842-10-35-5 a change in a reference index does not resolve a contingency, so the lease liability and right-of-use asset are not remeasured; the index is updated only when another remeasurement event, such as a modification or a change in lease term, occurs. If the landlord has not yet invoiced because the base is disputed, accrue the best estimate by debiting variable lease cost and crediting accrued rent payable, then true it up when the amount is agreed.

What inflation assumption should a 2027 budget use without an October 12-month CPI figure?

Use a documented substitute and label it. The last official 12-month all-items figure is September 2026's 3.7 percent. Once the October index level is published, a 13-month change from September 2025 to October 2026 scaled to twelve months is a reasonable derived estimate, as long as the model marks it as derived rather than a BLS statistic. The November 2026 report on December 10 will restore a clean 12-month comparison, so build the model to replace the placeholder when it arrives.

Once every clause has a page, the missing month stops being a surprise on an invoice and becomes a dated decision with a value, an entry, and an owner.
